title: Roth vs HSA: the triple-tax-free angle
audience: High earners with HDHPs who already max a Roth and are looking for the next tax-advantaged account
thesis: The Roth is tax-free twice — in and out. The HSA is tax-free three times — in, growth, and out for medical. That's a step the Roth doesn't have.

concepts.label: The Roth is twice tax-free
concepts.body: The Roth IRA is tax-free on the way in (you contribute after-tax dollars) and tax-free on the way out (qualified withdrawals are tax-free). Two tax events avoided. Growth is also tax-free — counted as the third 'Roth' benefit, but it's the same as the 'way out'.

concepts.label: The HSA is three times tax-free
concepts.body: The HSA is tax-free on the way in (above-the-line deduction), tax-free on growth, and tax-free on the way out for qualified medical expenses. Three tax events avoided. Contributions through payroll also dodge FICA — a 7.65% bonus that the Roth can't match.

concepts.label: The Roth beats the HSA after 65
concepts.body: After 65, the HSA loses its triple-tax advantage. Non-medical withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income — same as a traditional IRA. The Roth stays tax-free at any age, any reason. So: HSA first for triple tax-free, Roth second, traditional 401(k) third.
concepts.source: IRC §223(f)(2); IRS Pub 969; SECURE 2.0 RMD changes

sources: IRS Pub 969 — HSAs and other tax-favored health plans
